title: Ruling 2022-07: Renter Credit; Disabled Adult Receiving Social Security and Has Shared Living Provider
text:
Date: January 5, 2023

Written by: Emily Bergquist

Approved by: Craig Bolio, Commissioner of Taxes

This is a formal ruling for your client, [Taxpayer] (Claimant), regarding the availability of the renter credit for rent paid for his homeshare residence. This ruling is based upon representations in your email dated [date].

Facts 

1. Claimant is a developmentally disabled adult, collecting Social Security Disability, and living with a shared living home provider, paying the room and board rate set by Vermont Department of Disabilities, Aging and Independent Living.

2. Room and board for Claimant includes a bedroom, electricity, heat, bathroom, and meals and is the primary residence of Claimant. He has no other home to live in. He is not able to care for himself or live alone.

3. A shared living home provider receives room and board income from Claimant, and also a stipend for services from a mental health agency in Vermont that is paid from a Medicaid waiver.

Discussion 

You have asked whether a developmentally disabled adult, who is collecting Social Security Disability payments, and living with a shared living home provider, may claim a renter credit.

A qualified low-income individual who rents his primary residence may be eligible for a rental credit of up to $2500. 32 V.S.A. § 6066(b). The credit calculation is based on the income level of the renter and either (a) the rent paid (if the individual receives a rental subsidy) or (b) a

statutory calculation involving “fair market rent” as defined in federal law, if the individual does not receive a rental subsidy. Id.

There is nothing in the statute that would prohibit per se a developmentally disabled adult, who is collecting Social Security Disability payments, and living with a shared living home provider, from claiming the renter credit. (1) If the renter meets the low-income limitations of the statute, he is eligible to apply. 32 V.S.A. § 6062(b)(1). If the renter receives a rental subsidy, the amount of credit available is calculated based on the amount of “rent” paid directly by Claimant from Claimant’s own funds.

“Rent” for purposes of the credit is defined to include only payments “to the extent that the payments are solely for the right of occupancy” of the residence. 32 V.S.A. § 6061(7)(B). This means “rent” does not include payments for electricity, heat, meals, or any item other than the space occupied by the renter. If any of these other items are included in the payments made by the renter, they must be subtracted from the payments to determine the amount qualified as “rent.” The agreement between the social services agency and the placement home or nursing home, often specifies the amount to be paid as rent. This agreement should be provided to the Department with the renter credit application.

In cases involving a rental subsidy, only the amount “actually paid by the individual” claimant may be included as “rent” for purposes of calculating the credit. 32 V.S.A. § 6061(7)(B). This means that any payments made from funds of any other person or entity, even though paid on behalf of Claimant, may not be counted as “rent” for the credit calculation. Moreover, payments made to a trust or guardian or other person or entity for the benefit of Claimant, and not paid directly to Claimant, are not money of the Claimant himself; therefore, payments made from these other sources are not payments “actually paid by the individual” renter, and do not constitute “rent” for calculation of the credit. However, payments made from Claimant’s own funds will qualify as “rent” even if a guardian or other person writes the check or otherwise transfers Claimant’s funds to the landlord.

There are additional limitations that may reduce or bar a renter credit claim. A claimant must have been domiciled in Vermont for the entire taxable year, must have rented for at least six calendar months (not necessarily consecutive), and may not be a person claimed as a dependent by any taxpayer for Federal income tax purposes. 32 V.S.A. § 6066(c). In addition, if a claimant receives a rental subsidy, the credit is limited to a maximum of ten percent of gross rent paid. 32 V.S.A. § 6066(b)(1)(D). If the claimant's income is greater than the “very low-income” limit, the claimant is not entitled to a renter credit. 32 V.S.A. § 6066(b)(1)(C). Details of how to calculate a claimant’s income and how to calculate the renter credit amount may be found in the Department’s instructions for the renter credit claim form, Form RCC-146.

Note that the amount of renter credit or property tax rebate available to the shared-living host may be affected by the fact that Claimant is sharing the household and by the amount of space rented to Claimant.

General Provisions 

Issuance of this ruling is conditioned upon the understanding that neither the taxpayer nor a related taxpayer is currently under audit or involved in an administrative appeal or litigation concerning the subject matters of the ruling. This ruling is issued solely to the taxpayer and is limited to the facts presented, as affected by current statutes and regulations.

Other taxpayers may refer to this ruling, when redacted to protect confidentiality, to see the Department's general approach, but the Department will not be bound by this ruling in the case of any other taxpayer or in the case of any change in the relevant statutes or regulations.

This ruling will be made public after deletion of the taxpayer’s name and any information which may identify the taxpayer. A copy of this ruling showing the proposed deletions is attached, and you may request within 30 days that the Commissioner delete any further information that might identify the taxpayer. The final discretion as to deletions rests with the Commissioner.

You have the right to appeal this ruling within 30 days. 3 V.S.A. §§ 808, 815.

1 Prior to 2021 there was a limitation for claimants renting under a homeshare agreement. The prior law provided that a renter credit (formerly called a “renter rebate”) was based on 21 percent of “gross rent,” and “gross rent” was defined to exclude “payments made under a written homesharing agreement pursuant to a nonprofit homesharing program.” 32 V.S.A. § 6061(7). Beginning in 2021, that exclusion was removed from the law, with the result that payments made under such a homesharing program may be counted as gross rent if they otherwise qualify. 32 V.S.A. § 6061(7)(A), (B).
